title: JIT Compilation: Tiered Compilation, C1, C2, GraalVM
prerequisites: Java bytecode and class loading basics

progressiveExplaining.eli5: A tour guide has two ways to give a tour. At first, he reads every sign aloud as he walks (interpreting) — slow but starts immediately. After walking the same route many times, he memorizes a perfect script (compiling) and delivers it fast. If a route turns out to be complicated, he writes an even more polished script (deep compilation). If the route changes, he drops back to reading signs. The guide is the JIT: it watches how often code runs and upgrades the delivery method accordingly.
progressiveExplaining.junior: The JVM starts by interpreting bytecode, then the JIT compiler compiles hot methods to native machine code at runtime. HotSpot uses tiered compilation by default: C1 (client compiler) compiles quickly with moderate optimization, and C2 (server compiler) does deep optimizations for very hot methods. You can observe with -XX:+PrintCompilation and control with -XX:TieredStopAtLevel. GraalVM provides an alternative JIT (and an AOT compiler for native images). JIT means Java code gets faster the more it runs — benchmarks must warm up.
progressiveExplaining.senior: Architecturally, tiered compilation (default since JDK 8) has 5 levels: interpreted (0), C1 with/without profiling (1-3), and C2 (4). The interpreter collects profiling data (branch counts, type profiles via backedges and invocation counters); when a method crosses thresholds, it's queued for C1 (quick compilation with profiling), then promoted to C2 for full optimization using the profile. C2 performs aggressive optimizations: inlining, escape analysis, dead code elimination, loop unrolling, and intrinsic replacement. If assumptions break (e.g. a deoptimization due to a profile mismatch), the JVM deoptimizes back to an earlier tier. GraalVM's JIT is a C2 alternative written in Java, using a graph-based Sea-of-Nodes IR.
progressiveExplaining.underTheHood: The HotSpot compiler broker manages compilation tasks on compiler threads. C1 emits a linear-scan-allocated, straightforward native translation quickly. C2 builds a Sea-of-Nodes IR (Ideal Graph) with global value numbering, then applies the optimization pipeline (inlining with a call-site graph, escape analysis to scalar-replace allocations, loop transforms, and machine-code generation via a global register allocator). Profiling comes from interpreter and C1 counters stored in MDO (method data objects). Deoptimization (uncommon trap) reverts an optimized frame to an interpreter frame at a safepoint when a guarded assumption fails. Graal compiles the same bytecode with its own IR and can use partial escape analysis and more aggressive intrinsics.

interviewGotchas.question: Why is Java code slower at first and faster after warmup, and how does tiered compilation decide when to compile?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: This tests the interpretation→profiling→compilation model — interviewers want the thresholds and tier progression, not just 'the JIT compiles hot code'.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: The JVM starts by interpreting bytecode (level 0) so execution begins immediately. The interpreter (and later C1 with profiling) collects per-method data: invocation counts, backedge counts (loops), and type profiles of call sites, stored in method data objects. When a method's counters cross the compilation thresholds (e.g. -XX:CompileThreshold, plus tiered thresholds), it is queued to the compiler broker: first C1 with profiling (tier 2/3) for quick native code, then, if still hot, C2 (tier 4) for deep optimization using the collected profile. This lazy, profile-guided progression is why cold code is interpreted (fast startup), warm code gets quick compilation, and hot code gets maximal optimization — and why microbenchmarks must include warmup to reflect steady state.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: The naive answer is 'the JIT compiles everything at startup'. Compilation is demand-driven and profile-guided, happening after thresholds. Another trap: thinking compiled code is permanent — deoptimization (uncommon traps) reverts to interpretation when a guarded optimization (e.g. an inlined call's assumed type) is violated. Candidates who mention thresholds, MDO profiling, and deoptimization show real understanding.

interviewGotchas.question: What are C1 and C2, and how does GraalVM's JIT differ from HotSpot's C2?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: This tests knowledge of the compiler stack and the alternatives — interviewers want to know what each compiler optimizes for and where GraalVM fits.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: C1 (client compiler) is a quick compiler: it produces decent native code fast using a simple linear-scan register allocator, prioritizing fast compilation time (good for startup and short-lived processes). C2 (server compiler) is a heavyweight optimizing compiler: it builds a Sea-of-Nodes (Ideal Graph) IR and runs an extensive optimization pipeline — inlining, escape analysis, scalar replacement, loop optimizations, and vectorization — with a global register allocator. GraalVM's JIT (used with -XX:+UseGraal in some builds, and as the default in GraalVM's JDK) is an alternative to C2 written in Java, using a graph-based IR with partial escape analysis and a different inlining/optimization strategy; it also powers GraalVM Native Image via the same compiler in AOT mode. The choice affects peak throughput and warmup characteristics.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: The naive answer is 'C1 is faster than C2'. C1 compiles FASTER; C2 produces FASTER code. Another trap: assuming GraalVM is only for native images — it also provides a JIT compiler that can replace C2. Candidates who distinguish compile-time vs runtime performance and name the IR differences show real depth.
